network.target_molecule: Glutamate, represented as stereochemically unspecified glutamic acid
network.overall_strategy: This literature-constrained network contains 33 molecule nodes, 21 reaction nodes, and 10 distinct pathways. Seven pathways use experimentally accessible 2-oxoglutarate generated within an iron-promoted pyruvate/glyoxylate network; alternatives use acrolein/cyanide chemistry, electrical discharge, or impact chemistry. The pathways distinguish carbon-skeleton construction, nitrogen incorporation, reducing-equivalent supply, and release of free glutamate. They are distinct reaction sequences or experimentally distinct synthesis modules, not ten proven mechanistically independent, geochemically closed processes. Pyruvate, glyoxylate, acrolein, hydroxylamine, DAP, and preconditioned mineral availability remain conditional feedstock assumptions where indicated. Organic acids, ammonia, and HCN use reference protonation states; their actual aqueous speciation follows local pH. Explicit H+ and Fe2+ provide formal redox bookkeeping, not claims that acidic solutions or freely dissolved Fe2+ persist under every condition. Discharge, impact, and upstream iron-network nodes are explicitly lumped transformations rather than established elementary reactions. All settings are anoxic; surface UV is a resource or a degradation constraint. No enantioselectivity is assumed. A null environment_formed denotes external supply or formation in multiple settings.

molecules.common_name: ferrous iron; formal oxidized-iron product pool
hydrogen cyanide, representing the HCN/cyanide pool
diamidophosphoric acid; DAP acid reference form

reactions.name: Iron-promoted carbon-network production of 2-oxoglutarate
agents: Dissolved Fe(II) salts acting as coordination and reaction-network promoters

conditions.catalyst: Fe(II) salts; not assigned to a particular mineral
conditions.other: Anoxic heated pool or mineral pore with concentrated pyruvate and glyoxylate. Exact pH, iron loading, and branch-specific residence time are not supplied by the research summary. Shielding from excessive UV would limit competing photodegradation.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped aldol, rearrangement, redox, and decarboxylation network that generates 2-oxoglutarate among several organic acids. Acetate is a documented coproduct; CO2 and water represent aggregate decarboxylation and condensation bookkeeping. This is not a single pyruvate-plus-glyoxylate aldol reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) experimentally generated an alpha-ketoglutarate-containing network from pyruvate and glyoxylate with Fe(II) at 70 degrees C. This addresses the immediate alpha-ketoglutarate supply problem without treating it as an unlimited starting reagent. The selected outputs describe an aggregate module, not an experimentally established unique stoichiometric equation or complete product distribution. Formation and concentration of the starting pyruvate and glyoxylate remain unresolved upstream assumptions.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed hydrogen-driven reductive amination
agents: Supported nickel metal, experimentally Ni on silica-alumina

conditions.other: pH approximately 8; approximately 30 mM ketoacid; ammonia/ammonium supplied in bicarbonate medium; approximately 72 h. A gas-retaining cooled pore or confined aqueous compartment is required, rather than an open ambient-pressure pond.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the keto group and produces an imine/iminium population. Nickel activates H2 and hydrogenates the C=N functionality, releasing glutamate and water.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated glutamate formation under these H2/Ni conditions. H2 is the reductant and nickel is the catalyst, unlike reactions consuming reduced minerals. The study also found competing hydroxyacid formation; its substrate-panel yield ranges must not be interpreted as glutamate-specific yields. Compatibility with the upstream iron network requires cooling, conditioning, and H2 containment and has not been demonstrated as this complete sequence. Mayer and Moran (2022) identify unfavorable imine population and slow alpha-ketoglutarate amination as kinetic constraints.

reactions.name: Reductive amination on partially electroreduced iron-sulfide material
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS containing highly reduced iron sites; sacrificial redox-active material

conditions.other: Approximately 5 mM ketoacid, pH approximately 9.6, large ammonium excess, and approximately 48 h. The experimental solid was preconditioned near -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days. Fe represents the reduced-iron fraction rather than the bulk mixed-phase material.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-ketoglutarate-derived imine/iminium accepts reducing equivalents from reduced iron sites. Fe-to-Fe(II) oxidation supplies the formal two-electron reduction budget. Subsequent iron hydrolysis, adsorption, or precipitation is not resolved into separate solid phases.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported nearly complete alpha-ketoglutarate conversion using partially electroreduced FeS. The graph explicitly treats the reduced material as expendable, not as an indefinitely turning-over catalyst. Fe(0)/Fe(II) is a formal representation of the reduced-site budget, not proof that arbitrary native iron or untreated FeS reproduces the result. Natural generation and maintenance of the laboratory-preconditioned material remain an open upstream requirement; its regeneration is not established in this network.

reactions.name: ZnS-photocatalyzed reductive amination with sulfite oxidation

conditions.other: pH approximately 9; large ammonia/ammonium excess; UV illumination; approximately 4 h. Sulfite is a sacrificial electron donor and hole scavenger, not a catalyst.

reactions.mechanism: Photoexcited ZnS transfers electrons to the ketoacid-derived imine/iminium. Sulfite oxidation supplies the balancing reducing equivalents; sulfate is the formal fully oxidized donor product. No molecular oxygen is required.
reactions.reasoning: Wang et al. (2012) observed approximately 0.5% glutamate without sulfite and roughly sixfold enhancement with sulfite. Light-only and dark-ZnS controls did not produce detectable glutamate under the reported conditions. The route therefore requires an illuminated sulfide-bearing surface, not a dark deep-sea vent. Sulfate is included as the electron-donor oxidation endpoint; the supplied summary does not establish a complete sulfur-product balance. Low glutamate yield, ammonium excess, and photochemical destruction remain limitations.

reactions.name: Formation of the 2-oxoglutarate oxime

conditions.other: Hydroxylamine is added to the anoxic ketoacid-containing mixture. E/Z oxime configuration is not selected. Exact glutamate-branch pH is not specified in the supplied summary.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the keto carbonyl, followed by dehydration to a ketoxime.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) support amino-acid formation through oxime intermediates when hydroxylamine and Fe(0) are introduced into their iron-promoted network. This branch can use alpha-ketoglutarate generated in the same evolving mixture. The major geochemical weakness is the unestablished abundance of hydroxylamine, a criticism explicitly discussed by Kitadai et al. (2019). Hydroxylamine is therefore a conditional starting reagent, not silently generated from ammonia.

reactions.name: Zerovalent-iron reduction of the glutamate oxime precursor
agents: Fresh accessible Fe(0) surfaces; consumed reducing reagent

conditions.other: Anoxic iron-containing aqueous mixture. Surface passivation and iron precipitation can limit conversion. H+ denotes buffered proton equivalents, not a requirement for strongly acidic bulk water.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the oxime C=N bond and cleavage of N-O produce the amino acid. The overall oxime-to-amine conversion requires four electrons, supplied formally by oxidation of Fe(0) to Fe(II).
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) demonstrated amino-acid formation, including glutamate, with hydroxylamine and Fe(0), and individual-ketoacid experiments support oxime reduction. Separating oxime formation from reduction prevents the activated nitrogen reagent from being mistaken for an ordinary ammonia reductive-amination route. Fe(0) is stoichiometric; the graph does not supply a mineral-regeneration cycle. Fe(II) represents the oxidation-state product pool rather than a measured exclusive dissolved species.

reactions.name: Strecker feed-in synthesis of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated formaldehyde, ammonia/ammonium, and cyanide in a mildly alkaline pool, approximately pH 8-9. Volatilization and competing cyanohydrin or oligomer formation must be controlled.

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde and ammonia form an imine/iminium population that is trapped by cyanide to form aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is standard Strecker chemistry, consistent with the framework discussed by Van Trump and Miller (1972). The supplied research does not quantify this exact glycine-feedstock preparation under the stated pond conditions; its integration here is speculative rather than a claimed experiment from that paper. It provides a chemically explicit source for the glycine consumed in transamination instead of treating a pre-existing amino acid as a free resource.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to glycine
agents: Aqueous proton donors for acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis

conditions.other: A separate acidic heating stage, illustratively pH 1-3, followed by adjustment to the transamination conditions. Required residence time is not established by the supplied research.

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile hydrolyzes through an amide to the carboxylic acid, releasing an ammonia/ammonium equivalent.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydrolysis supplies the conventional amino-acid-release step of the Strecker framework discussed by Van Trump and Miller (1972). The supplied findings do not demonstrate this exact feed-in under naturally maintained acidic-pool conditions, so its environmental implementation is speculative. The alkaline synthesis and acidic hydrolysis stages are intentionally separated; efficient glycine production cannot be inferred merely from aminoacetonitrile formation.

reactions.name: Aluminum-assisted transfer of nitrogen from glycine to 2-oxoglutarate
agents: Al(III) supplied as a soluble aluminum salt, such as potassium aluminum sulfate

conditions.other: Hot acidic concentrated solution. Related experiments used approximately 0.2 M alpha-ketoglutarate, pH 5, and approximately 44 h. Aluminum availability requires an acidic niche rather than bulk alkaline seawater.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted imine chemistry transfers the amino group from glycine to the ketoacid, producing glutamate and glyoxylate without an external reductant.
reactions.reasoning: Stubbs et al. (2020) reported 44% glutamate in an Al(III)-assisted transamination experiment. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) reported related glutamate formation at pH 5 and 80 degrees C with concentrated alpha-ketoglutarate and glycine or aminoacetonitrile. The 44% yield is not assigned automatically to every listed condition. Glyoxylate regeneration creates a chemically required connection to the carbon-building module, but does not establish a self-sustaining cycle or remove the concentration burden.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic ammonia release from diamidophosphate

conditions.temperature: approximately 298-353 K across incubation and heating stages
conditions.other: Concentrated DAP-containing solution; hydrolysis can proceed through partially hydrolyzed phosphoramidate species. Complete conversion within the hydantoin-formation interval is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Successive P-N hydrolysis releases ammonia/ammonium and ultimately phosphate. This node aggregates intermediate phosphorus species rather than assigning instantaneous complete hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) used DAP as an ammonia source in the optimized alpha-ketoglutarate hydantoin experiment. The phosphate endpoint is chemically expected, but the supplied report does not quantify complete DAP hydrolysis or a geochemical DAP supply. This source module is therefore a conditional bookkeeping linkage. It prevents the phosphorus reagent from being mislabeled as a catalyst or omitted from the optimized route.

reactions.name: Decarboxylating Bucherer-Bergs formation of carboxyethylhydantoin

conditions.other: pH approximately 8.5; approximately 0.35 M alpha-ketoglutarate, 0.42 M cyanide, 0.5 M bicarbonate, and DAP supplied at approximately 0.7 M in the optimized experiment; approximately 21 days. Ammonia supply is represented separately by rxn_010.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition, nitrogen incorporation, decarboxylating chemistry, and carbonate-associated cyclization generate the hydantoin. The aggregate transformation incorporates an additional carbon into the protected product while releasing CO2; it is not simple reductive amination.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) obtained 96% 5-carboxyethylhydantoin under optimized conditions. This is a protected glutamate precursor, not 96% free glutamate. Cyanide and the ammonia source are consumed reagents. The detailed atom provenance is not established by the supplied summary, so the mechanism is represented at reaction-family level. Simultaneous accumulation of these high reagent concentrations and preservation for three weeks remain substantial environmental requirements.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylglutamate

conditions.other: Continued heating of the concentrated hydantoin-containing mixture, initially near pH 8.5. The experimentally reported overall hydrolysis stage lasted approximately 14 days.

reactions.mechanism: Water opens the hydantoin ring to the corresponding N-carbamoylated amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) describe hydantoin hydrolysis through carbamoylated intermediates. N-carbamoylglutamate is a mechanistically assigned intermediate here; the supplied summary does not give its independently measured concentration or rate constant. The persistence of 72% hydantoin after 14 days at 80 degrees C demonstrates that release chemistry is a major bottleneck, although the individual ring-opening and downstream rate contributions are not resolved.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic decarbamoylation to free glutamate

conditions.other: Continuation of the approximately 14-day hydrolysis stage. Carbon dioxide partitions into the bicarbonate pool according to pH.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis removes the carbamoyl group, releasing glutamate, ammonia/ammonium, and inorganic carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) measured 19% glutamate after the overall hot hydrolysis stage, with 72% hydantoin remaining. The 19% value belongs to the complete hydantoin-to-glutamate sequence, not to this isolated elementary step. Separate intermediate accumulation and decarbamoylation kinetics remain unresolved. This node explicitly distinguishes free glutamate from a protected carbon-and-nitrogen skeleton.

reactions.name: Internal-redox formation of N-succinylglutamate

conditions.temperature: 350-370 K, proposed hot-pool interval rather than a documented glutamate-specific optimum
conditions.other: Concentrated acidic ketoacid/ammonium solution, approximately pH 3-4 as indicated for better-characterized members of the reaction family. Competing pyroglutamate formation is possible.

reactions.mechanism: Coupled alpha-oxo-acid chemistry produces an N-succinylated amino acid with decarboxylation. One portion of the ketoacid inventory provides the succinyl group and internal redox compensation while another becomes the amino-acid skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Yanagawa et al. (1982-1983) identified N-succinylglutamic acid from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonium without an externally added reductant. The transformation consumes additional ketoacid; it is not an electron-source-free reductive amination. The supplied findings do not establish a glutamate-specific yield or optimum temperature. The stated hot-pool interval is a speculative environmental implementation of a supported reaction family.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic liberation of glutamate from N-succinylglutamate
agents: Aqueous proton donors for amide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Prolonged heating in an acidic concentrated pool, illustratively pH 1-3. This is not assumed equivalent to the strong-acid laboratory work-up; residence time and free-glutamate survival are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed cleavage of the N-succinyl amide produces glutamate and succinic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Yanagawa et al. (1982-1983) support the N-acyl precursor chemistry, but strong-acid processing, including 6 N HCl for related products, was important in amino-acid recovery. Efficient liberation under the proposed natural conditions is therefore speculative. This explicit bottleneck is necessary to avoid treating N-succinylglutamate detection as proof of substantial free-glutamate accumulation. Cyclization and decomposition may compete with hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Conjugate cyanide addition to acrolein

conditions.other: Approximately pH 9.2. The modern combined addition/trapping experiment used approximately 140 mM acrolein and 700 mM cyanide. Acrolein volatilization and polymerization are competing losses.

reactions.mechanism: Conjugate cyanide addition to the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde, followed by proton transfer, generates the 3-cyanopropanal skeleton. The aldehyde is readily trapped by further cyanide addition.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) identified acrolein-based chemistry as relevant to glutamate formation. Fernandez-Garcia, Grefenstette and Powner (2017) strongly support the combined cyanide-addition/trapping chemistry. Their approximately 95% result concerns the downstream cyanohydrin, not an isolated 95% yield of free 3-cyanopropanal. The aldehyde node represents the required transient functionality, and coincident concentrated acrolein/cyanide supply remains an assumption.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin trapping of 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Same approximately pH 9.2 cyanide-rich solution as rxn_016. Cyanohydrin formation is reversible and changes the concentration of free aldehyde.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, producing a hydroxydinitrile reservoir with the complete five-carbon framework.
reactions.reasoning: Fernandez-Garcia, Grefenstette and Powner (2017) reported approximately 95% cyanohydrin formation from the acrolein/cyanide system under concentrated conditions. This supports carbon-skeleton assembly but not an equivalent yield of glutamate. The intermediate must subsequently exchange its carbonyl-derived oxygen functionality for amino nitrogen and undergo extensive nitrile hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Strecker conversion of the cyanohydrin reservoir to an aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich, mildly alkaline aqueous solution, approximately pH 8-9. Conditions must permit cyanohydrin reversal and imine formation rather than irreversible trapping or polymerization.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation makes aldehyde available for ammonia addition and imine formation. Cyanide recapture yields 2-aminopentanedinitrile. The net step is not direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) proposed the acrolein-to-glutamate Strecker framework, and Fernandez-Garcia, Grefenstette and Powner (2017) support the required cyanide-containing aldehyde/cyanohydrin chemistry. The supplied findings do not quantify this isolated aminodinitrile-forming step under the stated conditions. Its integration is therefore conditional; the high cyanohydrin yield must not be propagated numerically through this nitrogen-incorporation stage.

reactions.name: Exhaustive hydrolysis of glutamate aminodinitrile
agents: Aqueous proton donors for nitrile and amide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Separate prolonged acidic heating stage, illustratively pH 1-3. Complete hydrolysis of both nitrile-derived groups is required; sufficient residence time is not established by the supplied research.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitriles hydrolyze through amides to carboxyl groups, retaining the alpha-amino group and releasing ammonia/ammonium equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the acrolein/Strecker framework discussed by Van Trump and Miller (1972) and supported upstream by Fernandez-Garcia, Grefenstette and Powner (2017). Natural exhaustive hydrolysis at the specified pool conditions is a speculative implementation, not a reported 95%-yield glutamate synthesis. Partial hydrolysis can accumulate glutamine-related or other amide intermediates. Water activity, acidity, temperature, and product stability determine whether free glutamate actually accumulates.

reactions.name: Electrical-discharge synthesis and aqueous recovery of glutamate

conditions.temperature: approximately 300-323 K in receiving water; nonthermal discharge excursions occur in the gas
conditions.other: Methane/nitrogen/water system with trace ammonia and electrical discharge. A locally reducing atmosphere, volcanic gas pocket, or analogous gas-water interface is required. Product recovery and any hydrolytic work-up are included in this lumped module.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical energy drives radical and ion chemistry in the gas, followed by aqueous reactions among a broad precursor mixture. Glutamate is an empirically identified endpoint; H2 is a formal net dehydrogenation product. No unique elementary glutamate mechanism or complete coproduct inventory is assigned.
reactions.reasoning: Ring et al. (1972) confirmed glutamic acid in methane/nitrogen/water/trace-ammonia discharge products. Schlesinger and Miller (1983) showed that strongly reducing gas inventories favor amino-acid diversity, whereas CO2 without H2 is ineffective for comparable complex products. This is direct reachability from simple feedstocks, but not a selective reaction or a quantified continuous source of free glutamate. The lumped chemistry may overlap mechanistically with the explicit Strecker branch; these are distinct network representations, not proof of independent microscopic mechanisms.

reactions.name: Impact-driven glutamate formation from bicarbonate and ammonium
agents: Fe/Ni-bearing meteoritic material; reactive iron is a reducing inventory rather than an established trace catalyst

conditions.temperature: Extreme transient impact heating followed by quenching into approximately 300-350 K water; the supplied summary does not specify the shock temperature profile
conditions.pressure: Transient high shock pressure followed by return toward ambient pressure
conditions.other: Surface denotes the impact-recovery setting, not a claim that shock conditions remain within ordinary pond limits. Bicarbonate, ammonium-bearing water, and meteoritic material are present. N2 may be present as atmosphere, but its incorporation is not assigned when ammonium is available.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped shock, redox, carbon-nitrogen assembly, and quench chemistry produces a complex recovered organic mixture containing glutamate. Fe(0)-to-Fe(II) is a formal reducing-equivalent endpoint; actual oxidized iron phases and intermediate organic structures are unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Furukawa et al. (2015) detected glutamate among impact-recovery products from bicarbonate-containing aqueous nitrogen sources and meteoritic materials. This supports access from inorganic carbon without externally supplied alpha-ketoglutarate. The supplied research gives no glutamate-specific yield, elementary mechanism, or complete iron-speciation balance. The graph therefore represents an empirical synthesis module, not a proven single stoichiometric reaction. Episodicity, rapid quenching, product work-up, and poor selectivity limit its interpretation as a sustained source.

pathways.name: Iron-built carbon skeleton followed by H2/Ni reductive amination
pathways.description: Pyruvate and glyoxylate generate an alpha-ketoglutarate-containing pool, which is cooled and exposed to ammonia and pressurized H2 over nickel. The modules are independently supported, but their complete serial integration and concentration balance are unproven.

pathways.name: Iron-built carbon skeleton followed by electroreduced-mineral amination
pathways.description: Alpha-ketoglutarate from the carbon-building network is aminated using preconditioned, highly reduced iron-sulfide material. The distinct reducing inventory is consumed, and its natural preparation is an explicit unresolved prerequisite.

pathways.name: Iron-built carbon skeleton followed by ZnS photochemical amination
pathways.description: An alpha-ketoglutarate-containing pool is cooled, adjusted to alkaline ammonium-rich conditions, and illuminated on ZnS with sulfite. This is a staged proposal requiring mineral and solution conditioning, not a demonstrated single-pot synthesis.

pathways.name: Integrated ketoacid-to-oxime-to-glutamate sequence
pathways.description: Iron-promoted carbon chemistry generates alpha-ketoglutarate, hydroxylamine converts it to an oxime, and Fe(0) supplies the four-electron reduction to glutamate. This has relatively strong experimental network integration but an unresolved hydroxylamine supply.

pathways.name: Strecker-derived glycine feeding aluminum-assisted transamination
pathways.description: Parallel precursor branches supply glycine from formaldehyde/ammonia/cyanide and alpha-ketoglutarate from pyruvate/glyoxylate. Their acidic Al(III)-assisted convergence gives glutamate and regenerates glyoxylate. The sequence is dependency-ordered assembly of both branches, not a claim that every successive reaction shares a single linear intermediate. An initial glyoxylate inventory is still required.

pathways.name: DAP-supported Bucherer-Bergs synthesis and hydantoin hydrolysis
pathways.description: A DAP-derived ammonia source and an alpha-ketoglutarate-producing branch feed concentrated cyanide/bicarbonate chemistry. Hydantoin formation efficiently traps the skeleton, but ring opening and decarbamoylation slowly release free glutamate. The sequence includes the parallel ammonia-source prerequisite.

pathways.name: Internal-redox N-succinyl pathway with conditional hydrolytic release
pathways.description: Alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonium generate N-succinylglutamate through decarboxylating internal-redox chemistry. Subsequent amide hydrolysis produces free glutamate and succinate. The precursor is supported experimentally, whereas efficient natural release of free glutamate remains speculative.

pathways.name: Alpha-ketoglutarate-independent acrolein/dinitrile pathway
pathways.description: Acrolein undergoes conjugate cyanide addition and cyanohydrin trapping. Ammonia-dependent Strecker exchange generates an aminodinitrile whose exhaustive hydrolysis gives glutamate. High upstream cyanohydrin yield does not establish comparable aminodinitrile or free-glutamate yield.

pathways.name: Simple-gas electrical-discharge reachability
pathways.description: Methane, nitrogen, water, and trace ammonia produce a recovered glutamate-containing mixture under electrical discharge. This empirically supported lumped pathway does not assign unobserved discrete intermediates or a selective free-glutamate flux.

pathways.name: Bicarbonate/ammonium impact-shock reachability
pathways.description: Impact energy and reactive meteoritic material convert inorganic-carbon and nitrogen inventories into a recovered organic mixture containing glutamate. The pathway is episodic and mechanistically aggregated, with unresolved glutamate productivity and detailed redox-product speciation.

evaluation.target_molecule: Glutamate, represented as stereochemically unspecified glutamic acid

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both modules have experimental support: Muchowska et al. (2019) demonstrate an iron-promoted network containing 2-oxoglutarate, and Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrate its H2-driven conversion to glutamate over suitable metals. rxn_001 is balanceable, but its inferred coefficients are not established experimental product ratios. The main integration gap is delivery of sufficiently concentrated 2-oxoglutarate from the upstream mixture to an active Ni/H2 system. The Biochemical label does not specify a physical environment, and the submitted network provides no reaction-specific pressure, pH, catalyst loading or residence time. Competing hydroxyglutarate formation should be included when assessing productivity.
suggestions: Parameterize rxn_001 with its Fe(II) inventory, approximately 70°C experimental conditions, residence time and measured 2-oxoglutarate production.
For rxn_002, document conditions comparable to the demonstrated pH 8, 22°C, 5 bar H2 and 72-hour experiment, or justify departures. Specify the active Ni-bearing material.
Demonstrate conditioning or transfer of the upstream mixture with adequate substrate retention, and measure amino-acid versus hydroxyacid selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019) provide strong evidence for glutamate formation using partially electroreduced FeS. The network appropriately acknowledges preconditioned mineral availability as conditional. The Fe/Fe2+ representation is acceptable formal electron bookkeeping, but it does not identify the actual reactive surface or establish that ordinary FeS or arbitrary bulk iron would reproduce the result. The literature used deliberately prepared material, alkaline conditions and substantial ammonium excess. Compatibility with the upstream iron-network mixture and the physical meaning of the Biochemical environment remain unspecified.
suggestions: Specify the reduced FeS phase, loading and preparation history, including the experimental benchmark of approximately -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days.
Provide the amination pH, temperature, ammonium concentration and residence time; distinguish formal Fe2+ bookkeeping from actual dissolved and solid iron products.
Test the conditioned upstream mixture or justify transfer, dilution and mineral contact sufficiently to support the proposed coupling.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfite-coupled net reaction is balanced and consistent with ZnS-mediated photoreductive amination. Wang et al. (2012) directly support glutamate production, with approximately 0.5% yield without sulfite and roughly sixfold enhancement with sulfite. Low yield does not invalidate target formation. An illuminated surface setting is appropriate in principle, but Surface alone does not establish photon delivery, ZnS availability, pH, ammonium concentration or sulfite supply. Transfer from the iron-network mixture also requires checking optical attenuation and effects on ZnS activity.
suggestions: Specify ZnS phase and loading, irradiation spectrum and flux, water depth, approximately pH 9 conditions, ammonium excess and sulfite concentration.
Quantify glutamate formation against photodegradation and competing reactions rather than treating substrate conversion as glutamate yield.
Establish that the upstream iron-rich solution can reach or be conditioned for the illuminated ZnS environment without losing its useful 2-oxoglutarate inventory.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported integrated upstream-to-target module in the submitted network. Muchowska et al. (2019) experimentally connect iron-promoted ketoacid production with hydroxylamine/Fe0 amino-acid formation, and individual ketoacid experiments support the oxime intermediate. Its advantage is demonstrated chemical compatibility, not the number or order of environments. The oxime identity and reduction bookkeeping are appropriate. Hydroxylamine is explicitly a conditional input, which is a legitimate scope boundary, but its environmental availability remains unestablished. The network still omits the concentrations, reagent-addition sequence, residence times and measured glutamate output needed for a highly confident environmental implementation.
suggestions: Attach the experimental conditions and addition sequence from Muchowska et al. to rxn_001, rxn_005 and rxn_006, including Fe(II), Fe0 and hydroxylamine inventories.

Write the checked coefficients explicitly: rxn_006 requires two Fe and four formal proton equivalents per oxime. Specify the corresponding physical iron phases without interpreting those proton equivalents as a required acidic bulk solution.
Clarify the conditional external supply of glyoxylate and hydroxylamine, and report free-glutamate formation in the integrated mixture rather than extrapolating from isolated-substrate conversions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strecker synthesis followed by aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis is chemically sound, and the glycine-to-2-oxoglutarate nitrogen transfer is balanced. Stubbs et al. (2020) directly support Al(III)-assisted glutamate formation, including a reported 44% yield under hot acidic conditions. Glyoxylate is correctly identified as the transamination coproduct. However, aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis conditions are unspecified, and the final step requires concentrated substrates and an available Al(III) promoter. The network does not show how the separate glycine and ketoacid feeds reach those conditions or whether residual cyanide and the iron-containing mixture alter promoter availability.
suggestions: Specify the pH, temperature and duration needed for rxn_008, including ammonia release and any necessary conditioning before transamination.
Parameterize rxn_009 using the demonstrated hot acidic regime, approximately 80°C and concentrated ketoacid solutions, with an identified Al(III) source.
Demonstrate compatible mixing or transfer of the two feeds. Mark the initial glyoxylate inventory explicitly so downstream glyoxylate production is not mistaken for a bootstrap source.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The network correctly distinguishes hydantoin formation, ring opening and liberation of free glutamate. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) strongly support this route: approximately 96% hydantoin formation, followed by 19% glutamate after prolonged heating, with 72% hydantoin remaining. Those results support target production but not efficient or complete hydrolysis. The individual rates of rxn_012 and rxn_013 cannot be inferred from the combined endpoint. DAP hydrolysis is balanceable, but its rate and ammonia-release profile must be compatible with hydantoin formation. The very concentrated, multiweek experimental regime is not specified or environmentally substantiated by the Surface label.
suggestions: Specify the benchmark regime: approximately 0.35 M 2-oxoglutarate, 0.42 M cyanide, 0.7 M DAP and 0.5 M bicarbonate near pH 8.5, followed by prolonged 80°C treatment.
Provide a physically justified concentration and retention mechanism, with nitrogen and cyanide losses evaluated during the thermal progression.
Measure DAP consumption, ammonia release, hydantoin, N-carbamoylglutamate and free glutamate separately; do not equate hydantoin yield with target yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Yanagawa and co-workers provide experimental precedent for N-succinylglutamate formation. rxn_014 is balanceable using two equivalents of 2-oxoglutarate, and its internal-redox strategy does not require inventing an external reductant. The principal weakness is rxn_015: formation of an N-acyl derivative does not establish environmentally effective release of free glutamate. Strong-acid hydrolysis was important in analogous literature experiments, while glutamate-specific liberation under mild conditions remains poorly constrained. The network acknowledges this conditional release, but does not provide conditions or kinetics that resolve it. Competing pyroglutamate formation also limits straightforward target accounting.
suggestions: Write the two-2-oxoglutarate stoichiometry of rxn_014 explicitly and specify the acidic formation conditions.
Demonstrate rxn_015 under a defined environmental pH, temperature and residence time; distinguish a laboratory strong-acid work-up from spontaneous environmental release.
Quantify free glutamate, N-succinylglutamate and pyroglutamate separately. Treat this branch as a derivative reservoir unless adequate free-target release is demonstrated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon-skeleton construction and aminodinitrile formula are coherent, and every listed step is balanced or balanceable. Van Trump and Miller (1972) support the acrolein-based proposal, while Fernández-García et al. (2017) provide strong experimental support for the cyanide-addition/cyanohydrin module. Their approximately 95% intermediate yield is not a glutamate yield. Conversion of the cyanohydrin reservoir to the aminodinitrile is plausible but less directly constrained by the supplied evidence, and exhaustive hydrolysis of both nitriles requires specified conditions. Partial hydrolysis can retain amide products rather than produce free glutamate.
suggestions: Document the initial concentration regime, including the demonstrated approximately 140 mM acrolein, 700 mM cyanide and pH 9.2 conditions, or substantiate a less concentrated alternative.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally substantial and connected, uses molecule IDs consistently, and contains several experimentally supported routes to stereochemically unspecified glutamic acid. The required balance assessment gives 11 reactions balanced as written, nine balanceable with coefficients, and one conservation violation: rxn_020. Correcting rxn_020 is mandatory; its failure does not invalidate the independently supported branches. Explicit coefficients should be added to the nine balanceable reactions. Literature alignment is strong at the reaction-family level, especially for the integrated iron/oxime module, direct reductive aminations, transamination and Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. However, the submitted reaction entries contain no attached citations or quantitative operating conditions. Surface and Biochemical labels alone cannot establish environmental consistency, catalyst availability or transfer feasibility. Principal network-level uncertainties are usable 2-oxoglutarate production in the upstream mixture, retention and conditioning between modules, concentration requirements, active mineral inventories, and release of free glutamate from protected intermediates. Conditional feedstocks are appropriately acknowledged rather than falsely presented as geochemically closed supplies; glyoxylate should nevertheless be explicitly marked as conditionally externally supplied despite its intermediate label. Formal protonation and iron bookkeeping are accepted, and neither stereochemical ambiguity nor the number of pathways, shared molecules or environments is penalized. P4 ranks highest because upstream-to-target chemical compatibility has experimental support. Problematic-reaction listings otherwise identify unresolved specification or integration issues, not additional conservation failures. The network is a credible conditional synthesis map, but it is not approved under the required overall-confidence threshold of 0.90.
